issues.legal_issue: An officer lacks jurisdiction to transfer proprietary rights when the statutory conditions for that transfer are absent because the landowner personally cultivates the land or the beneficiary is not a tenant.
material_facts: The landowner was found to be in cultivating possession of the land.
The person awarded proprietary rights was found to be a labourer, not a tenant or sub-tenant.
The officer made an order transferring proprietary rights to that person.
issues.conclusion: The officer lacked jurisdiction to make the order, which was a nullity and did not need to be formally set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 27(2) of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953, land under the landowner’s personal cultivation was excepted from the transfer to the State; under Section 27(4), the State could transfer the acquired interest only to a tenant cultivating the land. In the absence of the conditions necessary to exercise that power, the officer lacked jurisdiction. The Court also relied on Sheo Lal v. Sultan and Mohd. Murtiza Khan v. State of M.P., which support treating an order made without jurisdiction as one that may be ignored without first setting it aside.

predicates.special_act_transfer_proceeding: An officer conducted a proceeding under a special statutory scheme to transfer proprietary rights in land.
predicates.owner_personally_cultivated_land: The landowner personally cultivated the land at issue.
predicates.beneficiary_was_not_a_tenant: The person who received the transfer was not a tenant of the land.

issues.definition: When a special statutory transfer proceeding concerns land personally cultivated by its owner or a recipient who was not a tenant, the transfer order is without jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A title suit concerning immovable property is governed by the limitation rule for title suits, rather than the shorter limitation rule for challenging an order, when the adverse special-act order was made without jurisdiction and need not be set aside.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought a suit asserting title to immovable property affected by an order under a special Act.
The order had been made in favour of a person who was not a tenant, although the landowner was in cultivating possession.
The suit was dismissed by the High Court as time-barred because it had been filed more than three years after the order.
issues.conclusion: The order could be ignored as a nullity, so the suit was governed by Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and was not barred by the shorter periods under Articles 100 or 113.
issues.legal_principle: Where an adverse order must be set aside before relief can be granted, Article 100 applies, or Article 113 applies if no specific article governs. But an order made without jurisdiction may be ignored as a nullity, and a suit for title to immovable property in that situation is governed by Article 65. Sheo Lal v. Sultan and Mohd. Murtiza Khan v. State of M.P. support this distinction. State v. Sadh Ram and Gangu v. Mahanraj Chand were inapplicable because those cases did not involve the same circumstances in which the impugned order could be ignored without first being set aside.

predicates.immovable_property_title_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit asserting title to immovable property.
predicates.adverse_special_act_order: An order made in a proceeding under a special statutory scheme stood against the plaintiff's claim to the property.
predicates.order_made_without_jurisdiction: The officer made the order despite the absence of a statutory condition necessary to exercise the power.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff brings a title suit over immovable property affected by an adverse special-act order made without jurisdiction, the suit is governed by the title-suit limitation rule rather than the shorter order-challenge limitation rule.
